description: The Mars Global Digital Dune Database provides a comprehensive and quantitative view of the geographic distribution of dune fields from 65° N to 65° S latitude. The database encompasses ~ 550 dune fields, covering ~ 70,000 km2, with an estimated total volume between 3,600 km3 and 13,400 km3. Over 2300 selected Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) infrared (IR), THEMIS visible (VIS) and Mars Orbiter Camera Narrow Angle (MOC NA) images were used to build the database and are included in the ArcMap and ArcReader versions of the database. An initial data set of THEMIS band 9 spectral range images covering orbits 816-9601 (spanning 02/2002 - 02/2004 and Ls = 0.085º-358.531º) and comprising more than 30,000 images was chosen as the basis for the construction of the database. This provided ~98% nighttime and ~75% daytime areal coverage of Mars planet-wide. Images containing dunes were identified using THV (Interactive THEMIS IR Viewer written in Research Systems Incorporated's (RSI) IDL® software at the USGS in Flagstaff (www.mars-ice.org)). The 100 m/pixel resolution THEMIS IR images were used to locate potential dune features. The higher resolution THEMIS VIS and MOC NA images were used to assign Earth-based dune classifications (McKee, 1979). Where image quality allowed, slipface measurements based on gross dune morphology were digitized to represent primary wind direction responsible for that morphology. Azimuth values were calculated, from crater centroid to dune centroid, for dune fields located within craters. These indicators of wind direction can be compared to the included NASA/Ames Mars general circulation model (GCM) output (Harberle et al., 1999).

attr.attrdef:
Area of dune field polygon (km2) calculated in sinusoidal projection to preserve
          area. Datum is Mars2000 sphere with 3396190 m diameter.

Mean Dune Height by Type (m). The mean dune height (MDH1) calculation differs
          slightly between each region. The North Polar region (NP): Most of the dunes in the NP are
          part of large ergs, rather than small dune fields. Estimated dune height was derived in a
          variety of ways. (1) For areas with MOLA (512 pixels/degree) coverage, topographic
          profiles were measured across representative dune crests using an ArcMap tool. MOLA points
          were considered and only profiles in areas with sufficient MOLA point density were used.
          (2) In other areas, distance between barchan horns was measured. Terrestrial studies have
          found that dune height is roughly one tenth the distance between horns (for example,
          Finkel, 1959; Hesp and Hastings, 1998). Comparisons with Mars dune morphology suggest that
          the relationship may also be valid for Martian dunes (Bourke and others, 2006]. When a
          range of barchan sizes were present, a single estimate was made for the dune field. (3)
          When neither of these methods could be used, an average value was chosen based on the type
          of dunes and the height of nearby dunes. We also took onto account previous estimates of
          dune height (for example, Breed and others, 1979; Thomas, 1982; Lancaster and Greeley,
          1990; Bourke and others, 2004; Bourke and others, 2006; Ewing and others, 2009]. A value
          of 21 in this field means that an overall average was applied because a specific average
          was not calculated for this location. The Equatorial Region (EQ): All dune fields were
          placed into one of 5 groups based on common dune types within the dune field. Height for
          an individual dune field is defined as the average MOLA elevation minus the minimum MOLA
          elevation found in the dune field. Extreme MOLA elevation differences within a dune field,
          caused by underlying rugged terrain, could cause overestimation of dune height. To
          decrease the influence of rugged terrain, average dune height was calculated using only
          dune fields with a standard deviation (of elevation differences) equal to or less than
          that of the mean standard deviation of the interquartile range of the ~550 dune field
          polygons. The South Polar (SP): Dune height was calculated in a similar method to that of
          the EQ region. The SP region however included an additional dune form compared to the
          other regions (i.e., the “bull’s eye”), and therefore divided dune fields into one of six
          groups, rather than five groups used in the EQ region. The SP region also has a higher
          interquartile range, ~750 dune field polygons, compared to the ~550 dune field polygons in
          the EQ region.

This field has only been populated in the NP region. The term “density” describes,
          in a semi-quantitative way, the amount of surface area within a polygon that is covered by
          dunes. It is based on a parameter that we refer to as relative spacing, calculated by
          dividing the average dune length of a group of dunes by the average distance between the
          crests for these same dunes. It was not feasible to measure density for every dune field
          polygon, therefore, we measured it for about 10 dune fields and used those examples as a
          visual guide to assign a density value to the remainder of the polygons.

attr.attrdef:
Volume Method, raster clip (km3). This field has only been populated for the EQ
          region, which used ESRI ArcMap software to estimate volume using MOLA gridded topography
          elevations to define the base and upper surface of the dune field polygons. A 250 m buffer
          was placed around each dune field polygon so that when the MOLA elevation raster was
          clipped to the polygons, boundary pixels were included. The base of the dune field was
          assumed to be a plane of uniform elevation equal to the minimum elevation of the dune
          field and the MOLA surface was used as the upper surface. This assumption is most
          reasonable for dune fields that occur on flat regular surfaces. When dune fields occur in
          topographically complex environments, the assumption will cause overestimation of dune
          field volume. Thus, this value as a whole should be used as a maximum. Dune fields that
          covered less than 5 km2 were excluded from the volume estimates. This data field and data
          from Column J (Volume2) are of comparable volume estimates.

Volume Method, [MDH1]*0.001*[Area_sinu]. This field has been populated for the EQ
          and SP regions. [MDH1] refers to the dune field height (Column G), and is multiplied by
          0.001 to convert to km, and [area_sinu] is the area of the dune polygon calculated in the
          sinusoidal projection.

Volume Method, 0.5*[MDH1]*0.001*[Area_sinu]*[cover]. This field has been populated
          for the NP region. [MDH1] is the dune height (Column G), and is multiplied by 0.001 to
          convert into km, [Area_sinu] is the area of the dune polygon calculated in the sinusoidal
          projection and [cover] is an estimate of how much of the dune polygon is covered with
          dunes. This is a very rough estimate of dune volume. It assumes that if a dune were
          leveled, the resulting thickness is ½ of the estimated height. This method probably
          overestimates volume.

Volume Method: [EST]*0.001*[Area_sinu]*[cover] (km3). This field has been populated
          for the NP region. [Area_sinu] is the area of the dune polygon calculated in the
          sinusoidal projection, [cover] is an estimate of how much of the dune polygon is covered
          with dunes, and EST is equivalent sediment thickness (in meters, multiplied here by 0.001
          to convert to km). EST (Landcaster and Greeley, 1990) is the sediment thickness per unit
          area that would exist if dunes were leveled. Because we were estimating dune height,
          rather than recording dune spacing, we combined their equations and used EST =
          [0.0074*(DH-1.5666/0.01)]-0.87, where DH is dune height. Values of EST must be reduced in
          proportion to the surface area covered by dunes when using EST to calculate volume for a
          dune polygon that is not entirely covered with dunes. This method addresses the
          overestimation issue by arriving at a more realistic estimate of sediment thickness. A
          weakness of both this method and the method used in Column K (Volume3) is that a single
          average dune height is assigned to each dune field. For large dune field polygons, this is
          probably a significant oversimplification. If the erg is underlain by a layer (or layers)
          of sand, our method probably underestimates total volume.

Mean Dune Height 2 (m). Mean dune height (m) (MDH2) is based on measuring
          topographic profiles across representative dune crests using an ArcMap tool. In other
          areas, distance between barchan horns was measured. As with MDH1, dune fields were
          categorized into five and six groups based on dune types and a mean dune height was
          assigned to each category. Because profiles could not be measured on sand sheets, an
          arbitrary mean dune height of 1 m was assigned to the sand sheets.

Volume Method: [MDH2]*0.001*[Area_sinu]*[cover]*0.5 (km3). This field has been
          populated for the SP region. [MDH2] is the dune height (Column M), in meters and is
          multiplied by 0.001 to convert to km, [Area_sinu] is the area of the dune polygon
          calculated in the sinusoidal projection and [cover] is an estimate of how much of the dune
          polygon is covered with dunes. Although this is a rough estimate of dune volume, it does
          mitigate the overestimation due to underlying topography and is likely more realistic than
          the volume estimate calculation: [MDH1]*0.001*[Area_sinu] (Column J, Volume2). This
          estimation probably still overestimates volume because it assumes dune were leveled, and
          so the resulting thickness would be half of the estimated dune height.

Dune Field Average Elevation (m). The average elevation is given in meters. It was
          calculated for each dune field polygon using an ArcMap zonal statistics tool with MOLA
          gridded topography (in the Sinusoidal projection) as the value raster.

Slipface 1 azimuth. The azimuth, given in decimal degrees, is the average of
          individual slipface measurements. Where THEMIS VIS or MOC NA images of sufficient quality
          were available, polylines were drawn on slipfaces to measure the direction of wind
          movement at the time the gross dune morphology formed. The authors attempted to include
          enough slipface measurements to represent the general circulation and to give a sense of
          the complex nature of aeolian activity on Mars. The absence of slipface measurements in a
          given direction should not be taken as evidence that winds in that direction did not
          occur. When more than one direction was recorded, slipface measurements were grouped and
          an average for each direction was calculated. Slipface 1 is the direction with the
          greatest number of slipfaces used in the averaging process. Images were originally
          projected to ArcMap in the Simple Cylindrical projection using the Mars 2000 datum that
          did not account for change of scale in the length of a longitude degree as a function of
          latitude. Slipface azimuth shown here have been corrected for this effect and were
          calculated in decimal degrees in areocentric projection. For the NP region: only dune
          fields located in craters were populated. For other dune fields in the NP region, where
          boundaries are arbitrary and where polygons can be quite large, inclusion of an average
          slipface measurement was impractical.

Slipface 1 Count. The count is the number of individual slipface measurements used
          to calculate the average.

Slipface 2 Azimuth. The average of the direction with the second largest number of
          slipfaces used in the averaging process. It was calculated in decimal degrees in the
          aerocentric projection, and then corrected for longitude scaling effects as a function of
          latitude.

Slipface 2 Count: Slipface 2 Count is the number of individual slipfaces averaged
          to calculate the Slipface 2 azimuth.

Slipface 3 azimuth. The average of the direction with the third largest number of
          slipfaces used in the averaging process. It was calculated in decimal degrees in the
          aerocentric projection, and then corrected for longitude scaling effects as a function of
          latitude.

Slipface 3 Count: Slipface 3 Count is the number of individual slipfaces averaged
          to calculate the Slipface 3 azimuth.

Slipface 4 azimuth. The average of the direction with the fourth largest number of
          slipfaces used in the averaging process. It was calculated in decimal degrees in the
          aerocentric projection, and then corrected for longitude scaling effects as a function of
          latitude.

Slipface 4 Count: Slipface 4 Count is the number of individual slipfaces averaged
          to calculate the Slipface 4 azimuth.

Environment is a general description that divides dune fields into two main

attr.attrdef:
Crater Longitude (East). When a dune field is located on the floor of a crater,
          this field records the position of the centroid of the crater in decimal degrees east
          longitude. Only the North Polar and South Polar datasets include this value, this field
          was not populated for the Equatorial region.

Crater Latitude (Aerocentric). When a dune field is located on the floor of a
          crater, this field records the position of the centroid of the crater in decimal degrees
          latitude (aerocentric). Only the North Polar and South Polar datasets include this value,
          this field was not populated for the Equatorial region.

Crater area, in km2, is given when a dune field is located within a crater. If a
          dune field is located within a crater that is within one or more other craters, the
          innermost crater is considered to exert the most influence, so its area is used. Areas
          were calculated in the sinusoidal projection and are based on the authors digitized crater
          rims. Note that the term “crater” was used for simplicity, even though a small number of
          the circular depressions containing dunes may not be impact craters.

Crater diameter, in km, is given when a dune field is located within a crater.
          Diameter is calculated by formula based on the area of the crater. Note that the term
          “crater” was used for simplicity, even though a small number of the circular depressions
          containing dunes may not be impact craters.

Crater “Barlow ID”. Many dunes fall within the topographic catchment of impact
          craters. Dune field position within the crater and the relative area of dune fields as a
          function of crater size and morphology might be indicative of prevailing wind conditions
          at the time of dune formation or proximity to a source of sediment. As such, the authors
          have identified these craters for further study. Crater “BarlowID” is a unique ID number
          constructed after the method used by Barlow (2003) to assign ID numbers to craters.
          Longitude is listed first and both values are extended to one decimal place. The + or –
          sign of the latitude is given, indicating the break between the two values. Longitude is
          always four digits and latitude is always three digits, filling in with leading zeroes
          where necessary.

Crater Centroid to Dune Centroid, azimuth. This field is only populated for dune
          fields that are located inside craters. The azimuth is calculated in decimal degrees,
          based on the easting (meters) and northing (meters) of the dune centroid relative to the
          crater centroid. Latitude and longitude were areocentric as is standard for Mars. The
          centroid value was not calculated when a dune field was found to be centrally located
          within a crater, when the crater floor is extremely rough, or when there are many
          scattered dune fields within a crater. Note that the term “crater” is used for simplicity,
          even though a small number of circular depressions containing dunes may not be impact
          craters. The CDAz for the equatorial region was calculated a bit differently from the
          North Polar and South Polar datasets because the original database did not include crater
          coordinates. If a dune field was located within a crater in the EQ region, the equation
          used was: Azimuth1 = arctan(tan(azimuth)*cos(latitude)) Where Azimuth1 is the updated and
          corrected azimuth, tan(azimuth) is the azimuth done in simple cylindrical projection and
          converted to decimal degrees, and cos(latitude) is the latitude of the dune field
          centroid.

searchDescription: The Mars Global Digital Dune Database provides a comprehensive and quantitative view of the geographic distribution of dune fields from 65° N to 65° S latitude. The database encompasses ~ 550 dune fields, covering ~ 70,000 km2, with an estimated total volume between 3,600 km3 and 13,400 km3. Over 2300 selected Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) infrared (IR), THEMIS visible (VIS) and Mars Orbiter Camera Narrow Angle (MOC NA) images were used to build the database and are included in the ArcMap and ArcReader versions of the database. An initial data set of THEMIS band 9 spectral range images covering orbits 816-9601 (spanning 02/2002 - 02/2004 and Ls = 0.085º-358.531º) and comprising more than 30,000 images was chosen as the basis for the construction of the database. This provided ~98% nighttime and ~75% daytime areal coverage of Mars planet-wide. Images containing dunes were identified using THV (Interactive THEMIS IR Viewer written in Research Systems Incorporated's (RSI) IDL® software at the USGS in Flagstaff (www.mars-ice.org)). The 100 m/pixel resolution THEMIS IR images were used to locate potential dune features. The higher resolution THEMIS VIS and MOC NA images were used to assign Earth-based dune classifications (McKee, 1979). Where image quality allowed, slipface measurements based on gross dune morphology were digitized to represent primary wind direction responsible for that morphology. Azimuth values were calculated, from crater centroid to dune centroid, for dune fields located within craters. These indicators of wind direction can be compared to the included NASA/Ames Mars general circulation model (GCM) output (Harberle et al., 1999).

attr.attrdef:
Area of dune field polygon (km2) calculated in sinusoidal projection to preserve
          area. Datum is Mars2000 sphere with 3396190 m diameter.

Mean Dune Height by Type (m). The mean dune height (MDH1) calculation differs
          slightly between each region. The North Polar region (NP): Most of the dunes in the NP are
          part of large ergs, rather than small dune fields. Estimated dune height was derived in a
          variety of ways. (1) For areas with MOLA (512 pixels/degree) coverage, topographic
          profiles were measured across representative dune crests using an ArcMap tool. MOLA points
          were considered and only profiles in areas with sufficient MOLA point density were used.
          (2) In other areas, distance between barchan horns was measured. Terrestrial studies have
          found that dune height is roughly one tenth the distance between horns (for example,
          Finkel, 1959; Hesp and Hastings, 1998). Comparisons with Mars dune morphology suggest that
          the relationship may also be valid for Martian dunes (Bourke and others, 2006]. When a
          range of barchan sizes were present, a single estimate was made for the dune field. (3)
          When neither of these methods could be used, an average value was chosen based on the type
          of dunes and the height of nearby dunes. We also took onto account previous estimates of
          dune height (for example, Breed and others, 1979; Thomas, 1982; Lancaster and Greeley,
          1990; Bourke and others, 2004; Bourke and others, 2006; Ewing and others, 2009]. A value
          of 21 in this field means that an overall average was applied because a specific average
          was not calculated for this location. The Equatorial Region (EQ): All dune fields were
          placed into one of 5 groups based on common dune types within the dune field. Height for
          an individual dune field is defined as the average MOLA elevation minus the minimum MOLA
          elevation found in the dune field. Extreme MOLA elevation differences within a dune field,
          caused by underlying rugged terrain, could cause overestimation of dune height. To
          decrease the influence of rugged terrain, average dune height was calculated using only
          dune fields with a standard deviation (of elevation differences) equal to or less than
          that of the mean standard deviation of the interquartile range of the ~550 dune field
          polygons. The South Polar (SP): Dune height was calculated in a similar method to that of
          the EQ region. The SP region however included an additional dune form compared to the
          other regions (i.e., the “bull’s eye”), and therefore divided dune fields into one of six
          groups, rather than five groups used in the EQ region. The SP region also has a higher
          interquartile range, ~750 dune field polygons, compared to the ~550 dune field polygons in
          the EQ region.

This field has only been populated in the NP region. The term “density” describes,
          in a semi-quantitative way, the amount of surface area within a polygon that is covered by
          dunes. It is based on a parameter that we refer to as relative spacing, calculated by
          dividing the average dune length of a group of dunes by the average distance between the
          crests for these same dunes. It was not feasible to measure density for every dune field
          polygon, therefore, we measured it for about 10 dune fields and used those examples as a
          visual guide to assign a density value to the remainder of the polygons.

attr.attrdef:
Volume Method, raster clip (km3). This field has only been populated for the EQ
          region, which used ESRI ArcMap software to estimate volume using MOLA gridded topography
          elevations to define the base and upper surface of the dune field polygons. A 250 m buffer
          was placed around each dune field polygon so that when the MOLA elevation raster was
          clipped to the polygons, boundary pixels were included. The base of the dune field was
          assumed to be a plane of uniform elevation equal to the minimum elevation of the dune
          field and the MOLA surface was used as the upper surface. This assumption is most
          reasonable for dune fields that occur on flat regular surfaces. When dune fields occur in
          topographically complex environments, the assumption will cause overestimation of dune
          field volume. Thus, this value as a whole should be used as a maximum. Dune fields that
          covered less than 5 km2 were excluded from the volume estimates. This data field and data
          from Column J (Volume2) are of comparable volume estimates.

Volume Method, [MDH1]*0.001*[Area_sinu]. This field has been populated for the EQ
          and SP regions. [MDH1] refers to the dune field height (Column G), and is multiplied by
          0.001 to convert to km, and [area_sinu] is the area of the dune polygon calculated in the
          sinusoidal projection.

Volume Method, 0.5*[MDH1]*0.001*[Area_sinu]*[cover]. This field has been populated
          for the NP region. [MDH1] is the dune height (Column G), and is multiplied by 0.001 to
          convert into km, [Area_sinu] is the area of the dune polygon calculated in the sinusoidal
          projection and [cover] is an estimate of how much of the dune polygon is covered with
          dunes. This is a very rough estimate of dune volume. It assumes that if a dune were
          leveled, the resulting thickness is ½ of the estimated height. This method probably
          overestimates volume.

Volume Method: [EST]*0.001*[Area_sinu]*[cover] (km3). This field has been populated
          for the NP region. [Area_sinu] is the area of the dune polygon calculated in the
          sinusoidal projection, [cover] is an estimate of how much of the dune polygon is covered
          with dunes, and EST is equivalent sediment thickness (in meters, multiplied here by 0.001
          to convert to km). EST (Landcaster and Greeley, 1990) is the sediment thickness per unit
          area that would exist if dunes were leveled. Because we were estimating dune height,
          rather than recording dune spacing, we combined their equations and used EST =
          [0.0074*(DH-1.5666/0.01)]-0.87, where DH is dune height. Values of EST must be reduced in
          proportion to the surface area covered by dunes when using EST to calculate volume for a
          dune polygon that is not entirely covered with dunes. This method addresses the
          overestimation issue by arriving at a more realistic estimate of sediment thickness. A
          weakness of both this method and the method used in Column K (Volume3) is that a single
          average dune height is assigned to each dune field. For large dune field polygons, this is
          probably a significant oversimplification. If the erg is underlain by a layer (or layers)
          of sand, our method probably underestimates total volume.

Mean Dune Height 2 (m). Mean dune height (m) (MDH2) is based on measuring
          topographic profiles across representative dune crests using an ArcMap tool. In other
          areas, distance between barchan horns was measured. As with MDH1, dune fields were
          categorized into five and six groups based on dune types and a mean dune height was
          assigned to each category. Because profiles could not be measured on sand sheets, an
          arbitrary mean dune height of 1 m was assigned to the sand sheets.

Volume Method: [MDH2]*0.001*[Area_sinu]*[cover]*0.5 (km3). This field has been
          populated for the SP region. [MDH2] is the dune height (Column M), in meters and is
          multiplied by 0.001 to convert to km, [Area_sinu] is the area of the dune polygon
          calculated in the sinusoidal projection and [cover] is an estimate of how much of the dune
          polygon is covered with dunes. Although this is a rough estimate of dune volume, it does
          mitigate the overestimation due to underlying topography and is likely more realistic than
          the volume estimate calculation: [MDH1]*0.001*[Area_sinu] (Column J, Volume2). This
          estimation probably still overestimates volume because it assumes dune were leveled, and
          so the resulting thickness would be half of the estimated dune height.

Dune Field Average Elevation (m). The average elevation is given in meters. It was
          calculated for each dune field polygon using an ArcMap zonal statistics tool with MOLA
          gridded topography (in the Sinusoidal projection) as the value raster.

Slipface 1 azimuth. The azimuth, given in decimal degrees, is the average of
          individual slipface measurements. Where THEMIS VIS or MOC NA images of sufficient quality
          were available, polylines were drawn on slipfaces to measure the direction of wind
          movement at the time the gross dune morphology formed. The authors attempted to include
          enough slipface measurements to represent the general circulation and to give a sense of
          the complex nature of aeolian activity on Mars. The absence of slipface measurements in a
          given direction should not be taken as evidence that winds in that direction did not
          occur. When more than one direction was recorded, slipface measurements were grouped and
          an average for each direction was calculated. Slipface 1 is the direction with the
          greatest number of slipfaces used in the averaging process. Images were originally
          projected to ArcMap in the Simple Cylindrical projection using the Mars 2000 datum that
          did not account for change of scale in the length of a longitude degree as a function of
          latitude. Slipface azimuth shown here have been corrected for this effect and were
          calculated in decimal degrees in areocentric projection. For the NP region: only dune
          fields located in craters were populated. For other dune fields in the NP region, where
          boundaries are arbitrary and where polygons can be quite large, inclusion of an average
          slipface measurement was impractical.

Slipface 1 Count. The count is the number of individual slipface measurements used
          to calculate the average.

Slipface 2 Azimuth. The average of the direction with the second largest number of
          slipfaces used in the averaging process. It was calculated in decimal degrees in the
          aerocentric projection, and then corrected for longitude scaling effects as a function of
          latitude.

Slipface 2 Count: Slipface 2 Count is the number of individual slipfaces averaged
          to calculate the Slipface 2 azimuth.

Slipface 3 azimuth. The average of the direction with the third largest number of
          slipfaces used in the averaging process. It was calculated in decimal degrees in the
          aerocentric projection, and then corrected for longitude scaling effects as a function of
          latitude.

Slipface 3 Count: Slipface 3 Count is the number of individual slipfaces averaged
          to calculate the Slipface 3 azimuth.

Slipface 4 azimuth. The average of the direction with the fourth largest number of
          slipfaces used in the averaging process. It was calculated in decimal degrees in the
          aerocentric projection, and then corrected for longitude scaling effects as a function of
          latitude.

Slipface 4 Count: Slipface 4 Count is the number of individual slipfaces averaged
          to calculate the Slipface 4 azimuth.

Environment is a general description that divides dune fields into two main
          categories: those located within craters, C, and those located outside craters, N. A
          second descriptor is added for those located in Hellas basin, H, those located in Argyre
          basin, A, and those in Valles Marineris, VM.

Crater Longitude (East). When a dune field is located on the floor of a crater,
          this field records the position of the centroid of the crater in decimal degrees east
          longitude. Only the North Polar and South Polar datasets include this value, this field
          was not populated for the Equatorial region.

Crater Latitude (Aerocentric). When a dune field is located on the floor of a
          crater, this field records the position of the centroid of the crater in decimal degrees
          latitude (aerocentric). Only the North Polar and South Polar datasets include this value,
          this field was not populated for the Equatorial region.

Crater area, in km2, is given when a dune field is located within a crater. If a
          dune field is located within a crater that is within one or more other craters, the
          innermost crater is considered to exert the most influence, so its area is used. Areas
          were calculated in the sinusoidal projection and are based on the authors digitized crater
          rims. Note that the term “crater” was used for simplicity, even though a small number of
          the circular depressions containing dunes may not be impact craters.

Crater diameter, in km, is given when a dune field is located within a crater.
          Diameter is calculated by formula based on the area of the crater. Note that the term
          “crater” was used for simplicity, even though a small number of the circular depressions
          containing dunes may not be impact craters.

Crater “Barlow ID”. Many dunes fall within the topographic catchment of impact
          craters. Dune field position within the crater and the relative area of dune fields as a
          function of crater size and morphology might be indicative of prevailing wind conditions
          at the time of dune formation or proximity to a source of sediment. As such, the authors
          have identified these craters for further study. Crater “BarlowID” is a unique ID number
          constructed after the method used by Barlow (2003) to assign ID numbers to craters.
          Longitude is listed first and both values are extended to one decimal place. The + or –
          sign of the latitude is given, indicating the break between the two values. Longitude is
          always four digits and latitude is always three digits, filling in with leading zeroes
          where necessary.

Crater Centroid to Dune Centroid, azimuth. This field is only populated for dune
          fields that are located inside craters. The azimuth is calculated in decimal degrees,
          based on the easting (meters) and northing (meters) of the dune centroid relative to the
          crater centroid. Latitude and longitude were areocentric as is standard for Mars. The
          centroid value was not calculated when a dune field was found to be centrally located
          within a crater, when the crater floor is extremely rough, or when there are many
          scattered dune fields within a crater. Note that the term “crater” is used for simplicity,
          even though a small number of circular depressions containing dunes may not be impact
          craters. The CDAz for the equatorial region was calculated a bit differently from the
          North Polar and South Polar datasets because the original database did not include crater
          coordinates. If a dune field was located within a crater in the EQ region, the equation
          used was: Azimuth1 = arctan(tan(azimuth)*cos(latitude)) Where Azimuth1 is the updated and
          corrected azimuth, tan(azimuth) is the azimuth done in simple cylindrical projection and
          converted to decimal degrees, and cos(latitude) is the latitude of the dune field
          centroid.

searchDescription: The Mars Global Digital Dune Database provides a comprehensive and quantitative view of the geographic distribution of dune fields from 65° N to 65° S latitude. The database encompasses ~ 550 dune fields, covering ~ 70,000 km2, with an estimated total volume between 3,600 km3 and 13,400 km3. Over 2300 selected Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) infrared (IR), THEMIS visible (VIS) and Mars Orbiter Camera Narrow Angle (MOC NA) images were used to build the database and are included in the ArcMap and ArcReader versions of the database. An initial data set of THEMIS band 9 spectral range images covering orbits 816-9601 (spanning 02/2002 - 02/2004 and Ls = 0.085º-358.531º) and comprising more than 30,000 images was chosen as the basis for the construction of the database. This provided ~98% nighttime and ~75% daytime areal coverage of Mars planet-wide. Images containing dunes were identified using THV (Interactive THEMIS IR Viewer written in Research Systems Incorporated's (RSI) IDL® software at the USGS in Flagstaff (www.mars-ice.org)). The 100 m/pixel resolution THEMIS IR images were used to locate potential dune features. The higher resolution THEMIS VIS and MOC NA images were used to assign Earth-based dune classifications (McKee, 1979). Where image quality allowed, slipface measurements based on gross dune morphology were digitized to represent primary wind direction responsible for that morphology. Azimuth values were calculated, from crater centroid to dune centroid, for dune fields located within craters. These indicators of wind direction can be compared to the included NASA/Ames Mars general circulation model (GCM) output (Harberle et al., 1999).

description:
This Mars viewer highlights foundational controlled mosaics including Viking MDIM v2.1, MOLA/HRSC Blended Hillshade, THEMIS IR Day/Night mosaics and uncontrolled but high-resolution mosaics (Caltech Murray Lab CTX and Hirise PSP/ESP). Datasets have been compiled together and gratefully hosted as a Tiled Web Services by Esri.

Data descriptions and their creators are provided below:

IAU Mars nomenclature (credit: IAU/USGS). This set of layers are split into scale-friendly layers showing albedo features, small (lt 100km), large craters (gt 100km), and miscellaneous for the remaining features. Click on any feature to link to the IAU planetary gazetteer site hosted at USGS. Planetary nomenclature, like terrestrial nomenclature, is used to uniquely identify a feature on the surface of a planet or satellite so that the feature can be easily located, described, and discussed. This gazetteer contains detailed information about all names of topographic and albedo features on planets and satellites (and some planetary ring and ring-gap systems) that the  International Astronomical Union (IAU) has named and approved from its founding in 1919 through the present time. Definition of types: https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/DescriptorTerms.

Mars MRO HiRISE Uncontrolled PSP/ESP Equatorial Mosaic (credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona/USGS/Esri). This is very sparse equatorial uncontrolled mosaic for the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) using all available "red" Primary Science Phase (PSP) and Extended Science Phase (ESP) images as released through 2018. The HiRISE instrument, operated by the University of Arizona, is onboard NASA's 2005 Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO). Due to its extreme 0.25 - 1m/pixel spatial resolution, has attained about 3% coverage of Mars. These images are spatially located using initial pointing information for the low-resolution MOLA elevation model. Thus images can be horizontally misplaced by 100s of meters. All data used in the construction of this sparse HiRISE mosaic, were map projected at UofA, and have been publicly released and are freely available via the NASA Planetary Data System. This tiled web service, as hosted by Esri, is made available using lossy Jpeg compression using an 8 bit data range.

Mars MRO HiRISE Stereo DTM Orthorectified Images (credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona/USGS/Esri). This is very sparse mosaic for the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) stereo orthorectified images, red band, as released through 2018. The HiRISE instrument, as operated by The University of Arizona (UofA), is onboard NASA's 2005 Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO). Due to its extreme 0.25 - 1m/pixel spatial resolution, has attained less than 1% coverage of Mars (currently about 500 stereo pairs in total). These images are orthorectified (or terrain corrected) at native resolution (usually 0.25 - 0.5 m/pixel) through HiRISE stereo-generated digital terrain models (DTMs). These DTMs are made from two images of the same area on the ground, taken from different look angles. These DTMs and orthorectified images are generated by a variety a planetary facilities including the UofA, USGS, and others. All data used in the construction of this sparse HiRISE mosaic have been publicly released and are freely available via the NASA Planetary Data System. This tiled web service, as hosted by Esri, is made available using lossy Jpeg compression using an 8 bit data range.

Mars ME HRSC and MGS MOLA Blended Global Colorized Hillshade v2 (credit: NASA/JPL/ESA/DLR/USGS/Esri). This data product, now at version 2, is a blend of digital elevation model (DEM/DTM) data derived from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA), an instrument aboard NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft (MGS), and the High-Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC), an instrument aboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express spacecraft. The average accuracy is ~100 meters in horizontal position and the total elevation uncertainty is at least ±3 m. This blended DEM was then used to produce a hillshade colorized by elevation. This shaded relief (or hillshade) is just a visual representation for the original DEM using a simulated light source at 270 azimuth from north and 45 degrees up from the horizon. All data used in the construction of this DEM have been publicly released and are freely available via the NASA Planetary Data System and ESA Planetary Science Archive. When used, data credit should be: NASA/JPL/ESA/DLR/USGS/Esri. This tiled web service, as hosted by Esri, is made available using lossy Jpeg compression over an 8 bit data range.

Mars MRO Caltech Murray Lab CTX Uncontrolled Mosaic Beta01 (credit: NASA/JPL/MSSS/The Caltech Murray Lab/Esri). This is a preliminary uncontrolled Context Camera (CTX) mosaic, called beta01, that the Murray Lab at Caltech has created to (1) generate a list of orbits that will be included in the final mosaic, (2) decipher challenges involved with generating a product of this unprecedented scale, and (3) solicit feedback from the Mars science community for how best to generate the mosaic in a way that helps as diverse a group of scientists as possible. The CTX camera, as managed by Malin Space Science Systems (MSSS), has attained near global coverage of Mars at the scale of ~5 m/pixel. All data used in the construction of this CTX global mosaic have been publicly released and are freely available via the NASA Planetary Data System. The Murray Lab/Caltech grants free use of the beta01 version of the mosaic for all purposes. When used, data credit should be: NASA/JPL/MSSS/The Caltech Murray Lab/Esri. This tiled web service, as hosted by Esri, is made available using lossy Jpeg compression at an 8 bit data range. 

Mars MO THEMIS IR Daytime/Nighttime Near-global Mosaic (credit: NASA/JPL/ASU/USGS/Esri). The Mars Odyssey THEMIS IR Daytime and Nighttime near-global controlled mosaics were created by Astrogeology at 100m/p using data originally from Arizona State University (and NASA's Mars Odyssey mission). This represents all tiles that were completed as of Oct. 2018. It is fully-controlled and should closely align to the MOLA DEM/hillshade. This mosaic only covers from -65 to 65 latitude. For more background please see: https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/maps/mars-themis-controlled-mosaics-and-final-smithed-kernels 

Mars Viking Digital Image Controlled Mosaic (MDIM) v2.1 (credit: NASA/JPL/USGS/Esri). This global image map of Mars has a resolution of 231 m/pixel at the equator. The colorized mosaic was completed by NASA AMES which warped the original Viking colorized mosaic and blended it over the latest black/white Viking-based Mars Digital Image Model (MDIM 2.1) created by the USGS. The positional accuracy of features in MDIM 2.1 is estimated to be roughly one pixel (200 m). This new mosaic uses the most recent coordinate system definitions for Mars. As a result, MDIM 2.1 not only registers precisely with data from current missions such as Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) and 2001 Mars Odyssey but will serve as an accurate base map on which data from future missions can be plotted. All data used in the construction of this Viking global mosaic have been publicly released and are freely available via the NASA Planetary Data System. This tiled web service, as hosted by Esri, is made available using lossy Jpeg compression at an 8 bit data range.

Suggested citation: "Sun, V.Z., and Stack, K.M., 2020, Geologic map of Jezero crater and the Nili Planum region, Mars: U.S. Geological Survey Scientific Investigations Map 3464, pamphlet 14 p., 1 sheet, scale 1:75,000, https://doi.org/10.3133/sim3464."


The cratered highlands located northwest of Isidis Planitia have been recognized as one of the best preserved Noachian landscapes currently exposed on Mars, hosting a record of diverse surface processes, diagenesis, and aqueous alteration. This region has consistently been considered a high priority for landed mission exploration, and includes the anticipated landing site of the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover within Jezero crater. Past mapping efforts focused on Jezero crater and the area outside it, Nili Planum, have varied in spatial extent, map scale, and purpose, though none have provided a continuous, high-resolution geologic map at uniform scale connecting the two locations. This effort represents the first, large-scale, continuous geologic map spanning both Jezero crater and Nili Planum using high resolution images.


The map area contains the majority of both Jezero crater and Nili Planum at a publication map scale of 1:75,000, which was chosen to encompass the Jezero and southern Nili Planum landing sites under consideration for the Mars 2020 mission at the time of project initiation. Suggested citation: "Sun, V.Z., and Stack, K.M., 2020, Geologic map of Jezero crater and the Nili Planum region, Mars: U.S. Geological Survey Scientific Investigations Map 3464, pamphlet 14 p., 1 sheet, scale 1:75,000, https://doi.org/10.3133/sim3464."


The cratered highlands located northwest of Isidis Planitia have been recognized as one of the best preserved Noachian landscapes currently exposed on Mars, hosting a record of diverse surface processes, diagenesis, and aqueous alteration. This region has consistently been considered a high priority for landed mission exploration, and includes the anticipated landing site of the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover within Jezero crater. Past mapping efforts focused on Jezero crater and the area outside it, Nili Planum, have varied in spatial extent, map scale, and purpose, though none have provided a continuous, high-resolution geologic map at uniform scale connecting the two locations. This effort represents the first, large-scale, continuous geologic map spanning both Jezero crater and Nili Planum using high resolution images.


The map area contains the majority of both Jezero crater and Nili Planum at a publication map scale of 1:75,000, which was chosen to encompass the Jezero and southern Nili Planum landing sites under consideration for the Mars 2020 mission at the time of project initiation. This map covers an area that is exactly 1 by 1 degree (~60 by 60 km), spanning 76.8 to 77.8°E in longitude and 17.7 to 18.7°N in latitude. The primary base map used for this geologic map is composed of Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s Context Camera (CTX) images, compiled into a 6 meter per pixel mosaic. A nighttime Thermal Emission Imaging System 100 m/pixel image mosaic, digital terrain models constructed from CTX images, High-Resolution Stereo Camera topographic data, and High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment images also aided in unit identification and the assessment of stratigraphic relationships. We defined map units on the basis of various characteristics visible in the CTX data at map scale, such as their texture, tone, morphology, marginal characteristics, geographic location, and stratigraphic relationship to other units. Some units occur solely within Jezero crater, while Nili Planum contains a sequence of units that are present across the broader northwest Isidis region. Other units occur in both Jezero crater and Nili Planum, including bedrock, aeolian, and crater units. This map product provides a regional geologic framework that connects the geologic units across Jezero crater and Nili Planum and the history they imply, facilitates future local-scale observations by landed missions of the Jezero and Nili Planum region, and enables the extrapolation of units that have been defined primarily by mineralogic composition to areas where there is no existing orbital spectroscopic data

values.value: Light-toned, linear, commonly parallel low-relief ridges prevalent in local topographic lows such as impact craters, including along the interior margin of Jezero crater, and at the base of steep scarps throughout Nili Planum. Superposes other map units. Type area: lat 18.41°N, long 77.36°E

Indurated, rugged, moderately-to-heavily cratered, light-to-intermediate toned unit located along and on the northern Jezero crater rim and wall, along the interior margin of Jezero crater, and throughout Nili Planum. Overlies units Nnp1 and cr in Nili Planum and conformably overlies unit Nle in Jezero crater. Contains three different surface expressions with varying morphologic and erosional textures that grade into one another without clear or systematic stratigraphic contacts: a ridged expression in northern Jezero and northeastern Nili Planum, a heavily cratered expression in northern Nili Planum, and a light-toned rugged expression in southern Nili Planum (Figure 3). Type area: lat 18.67°N, long 77.57°E and lat 18.68°N, long 76.86°E and lat 17.77°N, long 76.86°E respectively.

Stratigraphically lowest unit in the map area and underlies all other units. Contains three different surface expressions: a high-standing rugged outcrop expression, a rugged, light-to-intermediate toned, moderately cratered, high relief expression with irregularly or poorly defined margins, and a smooth, dark-toned, lightly-cratered, low relief expression occuring in local topographic lows. No clear stratigraphic contacts are discernable between the three expressions. Hummocks (~100s of meters in diameter and 10s of meters high), ridge crests, and megabreccia occur throughout this unit. Type areas: lat 17.90°N, long 76.94°E; lat 17.74°N, long 77.18°E, lat 17.90°N, long 77.12°E respectively.

Rugged, heavily cratered, light- to intermediate-toned, planar unit, margins defined by low-relief, sharp, lobate scarps, located throughout Nili Planum and on the western rim of Jezero crater (lat 18.39°N, long 77.28°E). Erosional texture contains meter-scale blocks at HiRISE-scale. Caps lobate mesa sequences by overlying units Nue, Nnp1, or cr. Banding or stratification visible along some margins (for example, 17.87°N, 77.09°E). Type areas at different elevations: 18.19°N, long 77.01°E; 18.39°N, 77.27°E; 18.08°N, 77.26°E

Rugged, light-to-intermediate toned, high standing outcrops up to several hundred meters in height that occur throughout Nili Planum and along the Jezero crater rim and interior margin. Peaks are generally rugged (for example, 18.602°N, 77.031°E), with dark-toned and smooth slopes that sometimes expose underlying unit Nue (Figure 6). Nonconformable contacts with unit Nue occur at different elevations (Cross Section B-B'). Type area: lat 17.81°N, long 76.92°E.
Rugged, light- to intermediate-toned, relatively high-relief scarps surrounding circular or quasicircular depressions >500 m in diameter. Type area: lat 18.04°N, long 77.51°E

Smooth, intermediate-toned, commonly featureless unit with rare dark-toned occurrences (for example, 17.85°N, 77.50°E) that occurs predominantly on the steep interior slopes of Jezero crater and Sedona crater, on Nili Planum east of Sedona crater, and in local depressions. Type area: lat 17.84°N, long 77.68°E

Rugged, lightly cratered, light- to intermediate-toned unit concentrically exposed on the floor of Jezero adjacent to unit Njf. Topographically lower than adjacent unit Nue. Contains NE-SW trending ridges that extend several hundred meters in length. When present, impact craters are typically >200 m in diameter. Type area: lat 18.28°N, long 77.49°E

Rugged, hummocky, variably-toned unit that occurs around Sedona crater, Angelica crater, and an unnamed crater (17.87°N, 77.30°E). Contains frequent lineations and rare lobate scarps. Type area: lat 17.75°N, long 77.50°E

Lightly cratered, intermediate-toned, stratified unit with margins defined by sharp scarps, located at the mouth of Neretva Vallis on the western portion of Jezero crater's floor. Occurs at higher elevation than unit NHjf1 (18.58°N, 77.48°E). Contain rugged arcuate ridges and troughs that branch out from nodes and define several overlapping lobes (Figure 7). Meter-scale sequences of alternating light and dark strata as well as some curvilinear strata (18.48°N, 77.39°E; 18.47°N, 77.37°E). Forms isolated outcrops that are <50 m in height on the Jezero crater floor east of the main unit. Some outcrops exhibit parallel stratification on their slopes (18.43°N, 77.36°E), while others do not exhibit obvious visible stratification at map scale (for example, 18.47°N, 77.50°E). Type areas: lat 18.49°N, long 77.36°E and lat 18.47°N, long 77.50°E.

Rugged, moderately-to-heavily cratered, light- to dark-toned, planar unit with margins defined by low-relief, sharp, lobate scarps, forms the central portion of the Jezero crater floor and overlies and embays units Nue and Nle, respectively. Most impact craters on this surface are <200 m. Can have dark, smooth surface texture, especially near contact with unit NHjf2. Type area: lat 18.43°N, long 77.65°E.

Rugged, light- to intermediate-toned, low-relief hillocks within Sedona crater and Angelica crater. Hillocks range from several hundred meters2 up to 1.5 km2 in area and are several tens of meters in height. Type area: lat 17.84°N, long 77.56°E

Smooth, sparsely cratered, light-toned unit located on the northwestern floor of Jezero crater. Northeastern portion contains ridges that trend from NE to SW (18.60°N, 77.59°E), similar to the ridged Nue unit nearby. Southwestern portion contains semi-arcuate ridges and troughs (18.59°N, 77.47°E). Meter-scale stratification occasionally visible along the edges of the unit and within terraced knobby outcrops (for example, 18.60°N, 77.55°E). Type area: lat 18.59°N, long 77.47°E.

Smooth, rarely cratered, dark-toned unit with margins defined by low-relief scarps. Outcrops within and near Neretva Vallis are triangular-shaped, with rare stratification (18.56°N, 76.83°E), and overlie and infill parts of Neretva Vallis. Outcrops near Una Vallis occur in depressions, one of which is the end point for Una Vallis, and contain stratification at HiRISE scale (18.33°N, 77.09°E). Type area: 18.47°N, long 76.88°E

Low-relief ridges are up to several hundred meters in length and spacing is on the order of 10s of meters. Bifurcations and overlapping ridges are common. Crestlines trend approximately N-S, but can vary locally. Low-relief ridges occur in fields up to several km2 in area.

Occurs at elevations ranging from -2707 m within Jezero to -1787 m in Nili Planum. Ridged expression has ridges trending northeast to southwest, and overlies the Jezero crater rim (18.56°N, 77.28°E). Heavily cratered expression has a rougher, heavily cratered surface with no preferential direction indicated by erosional textures. Light-toned rugged expression has a moderately rough, cratered surface with variegated tones and very sharply defined ridged margins that often forms linear outcrops extending up to 5 kilometers in length (17.78°N, 77.31°E) and can be associated with raised linear ridges in unit Nnp1 (for example, 18.19°N, 77.06°E; 17.86°N, 77.03°E). Associated with olivine and variable carbonate (Goudge and others, 2015; Bramble and others, 2017). Previously mapped as the 'fractured unit' by Bramble and others (2017), and inside Jezero crater as the 'mottled terrain' by Goudge and others (2015).

Commonly associated with Fe/Mg clay, low calcium pyroxene, rare Al clay (Ehlmann and Mustard, 2012; Bramble and others, 2017; Scheller and Ehlmann, 2020). Previously mapped as the 'basement unit' by Bramble and others (2017) and 'basement group' by Scheller and Ehlmann (2020).

Outcrops as small as 0.02 km2 or as large as 23 km2 and span 241 m of elevation range (-2067 to -1826 m elevation) within the map area. Associated with mafic composition (Bramble and others, 2017). Previously mapped as the 'thin capping unit' by Goudge and others (2015) and as the 'capping unit' by Bramble and others (2017).

Outcrops range from 0.03 to 10 km2 in areal extent. Smaller outcrops visible at HiRISE scale and overlie unit Nue (for example, 17.87°N, 77.25°E; 18.10°N, 77.31°E). Stratification only rarely observed at HiRISE-scale (17.88°N, 77.18°E; 17.86°N, 77.09°E). Some outcrops have been previously mapped as basement 'crustal mounds' by Bramble and others (2017).

Meter to decimeter-scale stratification is observed in the interior rim wall of Sedona and Angelica craters. Stratification is present in the Jezero crater rim and shows evidence for warping and faulting at HiRISE-scale (18.46°N, 77.26°E). Megabreccia identified in Jezero's cr at HiRISE-scale (Figure 2).

Unit is exposed in erosional windows through the overlying unit Njf (for example, 18.44°N, 77.44°E and 18.33°N, 77.73°E). Associated with olivine and variable carbonate (Goudge and others, 2015). Previously mapped as the 'light-toned floor unit' and 'dusty light-toned floor unit' by Goudge and others (2015).
Most lineations around Sedona and Angelica crater are oriented radial to crater center; some lineations around Sedona crater follow the trace of lobate scarps (for example, 17.83°N,  77.43°E).
Associated with Fe/Mg clay and carbonate (Ehlmann and others, 2008; Goudge and others, 2015; Horgan and others, 2019). Previously mapped as the 'western fan deposit' by Goudge and others (2015).
Associated with mafic composition (Goudge and others, 2015). Previously mapped as the 'volcanic floor unit' by Goudge and others (2015).

Lacks the branching channels of unit NHjf2. Associated with Fe/Mg clay and carbonate (Ehlmann and others, 2008; Goudge and others, 2015; Horgan and others, 2019). Previously mapped as the 'northern fan deposit' by Goudge and others (2015).

One outcrop (18.47°N,  76.89°E) has a clear apex marking the transition from elongate deposit to triangular-shaped deposit. Previously mapped as the 'dark, smooth volcanic unit' by Goudge and others (2015).
Amazonian-aged bedforms and transverse aeolian ridges (TARs) composed of unconsolidated sediment oriented orthogonal to the dominant east-west wind direction (Day and Dorn, 2019).

Volcanic ash deposit that drapes underlying units Nnp1, cr, and Nle. Could also be other clastic deposit of volcanic or eolian origin. The three distinct surface expressions could result from differential erosion or cementation, as no clear or systematic stratigraphic contacts are discernable between the three surface expressions. Ridges in the ridged Nue unit are yardangs (Day and Dorn, 2019). Long linear occurrences of the light-toned rugged Nue unit could have formed through infilling of preexisting fractures created by the Isidis impact.

Crustal rocks of undetermined origin, representing pre-Isidis crust, syn-Isidis impact products, and syn-Jezero impact products. Nnp1 was the target rock for the Jezero impact. Megabreccias represent pre-Isidis and pre-Jezero crust. The smooth dark-toned surface expression could be lower-relief portions of these crustal rocks that have been preferentially covered by eroded sediments from local or regional units or mantled by an unconsolidated dark, smooth deposit (possibly su) of unknown origin. Linear ridge crests are inferred to be filled or cemented fractures.

Volcanic ash or eolian airfall deposit emplaced during the Late Noachian, possibly in multiple, localized episodes of deposition, that drapes underlying topography, for example on the Jezero crater rim. Correlates with unit Njf based on common stratigraphic position and shared textural and morphologic characteristics.

Indurated remnant deposits of a more extensive unit of undetermined sedimentary or volcanic origin that was emplaced during the Late Noachian. Nonconformably deposited on top of unit Nue, as contacts between the two units occur at different elevations. Subsequently eroded to its current form as isolated outcrops.

Undifferentiated target rock exposed and uplifted during impact. Target rock was unit Nnp1 for Jezero (cross sections). High standing outcrops of unit cr by the western and southern Jezero crater walls contain megabreccia and represent collapsed portions of the transient crater rim (cross section B-B’).
Sediments contributed from mass wasting, a widespread deposit of volcanic, or eolian origin, or residual accumulation of sand, pebbles, and cobbles due to deflation of the landscape.

Volcanic ash deposit, similar to the origin of unit Nue. Could also be other clastic deposit of volcanic or eolian origin. Either deposited into an existing lake within Jezero or subsequently altered by later lacustrine processes during emplacement of units NHjf1 and NHjf2. Underlies unit Nue based on its consistently lower elevation. Ridges are yardangs (Day and Dorn, 2019).
Sediments and undifferentiated target rock displaced during impact ejection. Target rock was unit Nnp1 for Jezero (cross sections).

Deltaic fan deposits emplaced during the Late Noachian to Early Hesperian, postdating and overlying portions of unit NHjf1. Presence of inlet channels (Neretva, Sava Valles) and an outlet channel (Pliva Vallis) suggests deposition into a lacustrine environment. Rugged arcuate ridges are inverted channels based on their association with the fan deposit and radiation out from various  nodes. Overlapping lobes represent branching channel deposits and distinct episodes of sediment deposition (Figure 7). Isolated outcrops could be remnants of the main delta deposit, much of which has been eroded since initial deposition.

Volcanic ash or eolian airfall deposit that drapes underlying topography. Correlates with unit Nnp2 based on common stratigraphic position and shared textural and morphologic characteristics. Emplaced during the Late Noachian before deposition of unit NHjf1. May have been modified by subsequent lacustrine activity during deposition of units NHjf1 and NHjf2. Dark, smooth surface texture near unit NHjf2 is due to a dark mantle deposit or erosional lag derived from erosion of unit NHjf2. Previously interpreted by Schon and others (2012) and Goudge and others (2015) as an extrusive volcanic flow.

Degraded deltaic or lacustrine deposit emplaced during the Late Noachian before deposition of unit NHjf2. Represents an older episode of deposition from Neretva Vallis, given its spatial disconnect from Sava Vallis, proximity to unit NHjf2, and arcuate ridges in the southwestern outcrop that are inverted channels extending away from the direction of Neretva Vallis. Previously interpreted by Goudge and others (2015) as an older, degraded deposit from Sava Vallis.

Mass wasted blocks from unit cr, or deposits of undetermined sedimentary or volcanic origin, emplaced within Sedona crater and Angelica crater during the Late Noachian and subsequently eroded to their current form. May be correlative with Nue.

Alluvial/fluvial deposits emplaced during the Early to Late Hesperian, likely during the later stages of fluvial activity in Neretva Vallis and subsequently mantled by smooth, dark-toned mantle or erosional lag deposit.
